headline: Massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by Dec. 31
dek: A planned change to the state’s financial-monitoring process would move public warnings earlier for private institutions that may not have resources to meet student obligations for 18 months.
body: Massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities found to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice in December, no later than Dec. 31. The planned change is part of an update to the state’s Financial Assessment and Risk Monitoring process, or FARM, and is intended to give students, employees and communities more time to plan before the spring semester is well underway. The [Massachusetts Board of Higher Education’s Sept. 29 FARM update](https://www.mass.edu/bhe/documents/2026-9-26-FARM-Update.pdf) describes the requirement as a fiscal-year 2027 enhancement. [WBUR reported](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools) on the board discussion.

The notice would not mean that a college had decided to close, and the state did not identify a new institution as being in that position in the materials reviewed for this report. Instead, the proposed timing would make a school’s financial risk public when the Department of Higher Education determines that it may not have sufficient resources to fulfill its obligations to enrolled and admitted students for the next 18 months. That distinction matters: the policy is designed to provide an earlier warning and a chance to arrange transfers or teach-outs, not to announce that every school receiving a notice will shut down.

The Board of Higher Education and the department already operate an annual system for screening the finances of private institutions. The [department’s FARM overview](https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp) says the process is intended to identify institutions at risk of imminent closure and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities. Under the planned enhancement, the public notice would arrive in December rather than after colleges have moved deeper into the academic year and students have made deposits or settled into spring plans.

The board’s update says the earlier notice is meant to avoid spring postings that are less useful for planning. WBUR reported that Board Chair Chris Gabrieli said current rules allow determinations after Dec. 1, the annual threshold date used to evaluate whether an institution can continue through the current and following academic year. Department Commissioner Noe Ortega told the board that the proposed Dec. 31 deadline would help officials support students while institutions are still making decisions about the future.

The state’s existing legal framework requires more than a warning. Under [Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 69, Section 31B](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleXII/Chapter69/Section31B), a private institution must immediately notify the board about known liabilities or risks reasonably likely to cause an imminent closure or interfere with obligations to current and admitted students. If the board determines that an institution may be at risk, the school must provide information for the review and prepare a contingency plan. That plan must address how students can complete their programs, how records would be preserved, student-loan information, financial and accreditation disclosures, and refunds for eligible student deposits.

The proposed December notice is one part of a broader effort to start that planning earlier. The FARM update says the department wants to condense contingency planning from three phases to two, with earlier work on transfer agreements and curriculum maps for programs that have specialized accreditation, licensure requirements or few transfer options. It also calls for earlier detail on community communications and employee-reduction plans if a closure occurs. All institutions, regardless of whether they are currently in the FARM process, would be encouraged to develop transfer memorandums of understanding and curriculum maps with partner schools.

The department also says it needs more capacity to assess financial risk. The board document outlines plans to procure outside accounting and financial-services consultants as needed and to explore additional full-time positions, including audit expertise. The stated rationale is that worsening market conditions may put more institutions at risk while the department relies heavily on information supplied by colleges rather than independently verified data. The planned support would supplement, not replace, the department’s existing review process.

The issue has become more immediate in Massachusetts after Anna Maria College in Paxton and Hampshire College in Amherst announced in April that they planned to close amid financial struggles, according to WBUR. The department’s public FARM page says it is working with Hampshire to help students complete degrees or transfer by the end of 2026, while the state has also listed Anna Maria among institutions involved in recent financial-assessment communications. Those cases illustrate why the timing of a warning can affect more than enrollment: students may need to compare credits and programs, faculty and staff may need to seek work, and host communities may have to plan for the loss of an institution.

The next step is implementation of the fiscal-year 2027 FARM enhancements and continued board oversight. The public materials do not name colleges that would receive a December notice, and they do not establish that a closure is imminent at any particular campus. For students and families, the practical takeaway is to watch both their institution’s financial communications and the department’s [public notifications page](https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp), where Massachusetts posts notices related to institutional financial condition and risk. Earlier disclosure could give affected students more choices, but it cannot remove the financial pressures facing small private colleges.
